post:
A composite, not a client: a 60-person firm in Los Angeles with one internal IT person.

Her week used to be password resets, laptop setup, and the same printer issue on a loop. Most of that is now automated or self-service. What filled the gap: a Microsoft 365 permissions mess, a cyber insurance questionnaire nobody can answer, three SaaS subscriptions finance didn't know it was paying for, and a request to switch on an AI assistant that can read everything she hasn't locked down.

Same headcount. Completely different job.

Note what that does to the scoreboard. Her ticket count went down. Her week got harder.

Before your next hire or renewal, read your last 50 tickets and mark the ones that repeated. Then ask what you would actually be paying for if those repeats vanished tomorrow.

Whatever is left is your real IT strategy. Staff for that part. Buy the rest.
headline: Before your next IT hire or renewal
core_idea: Automation removed the repetitive tier of IT work rather than IT jobs — which quietly breaks ticket volume as a staffing and pricing signal, because the tickets that remain are the ambiguous ones. The executive exercise is to separate repetitive work from judgment work and decide which one you buy and which one you hire.

channels.linkedin:
Automation didn't eliminate IT roles. It eliminated the bottom tier of IT work, and most org charts are still sized as if that tier exists.

Password resets. New-hire provisioning. Reimaging a laptop. The fourth VPN ticket this week from the same department. Scripted and agent-assisted workflows absorb more of that volume every quarter, and you can watch it happen in your own queue without an industry report telling you so.

What remains does not compress. Identity architecture. Microsoft 365 permission design. Cloud spend nobody owns. Incident judgment under pressure. And a category that was not on the 2019 org chart: deciding what an AI agent is allowed to reach, and who owns the machine identity it authenticates as.

There is a measurement trap inside this shift. When the easy tier leaves the queue, the tickets left behind are the ambiguous ones. Volume falls while difficulty rises. A team sized by ticket count — or an MSP priced by it — is being measured on the part of the work that is going away.

Four things worth doing before your next IT hire or MSP renewal:

1. Read your last 50 tickets. The tickets, not the dashboard.
2. Mark every one that repeated.
3. Price the repetitive tier separately from the judgment tier.
4. Hire for judgment. Buy the rest as a service.

Steps one and two take an afternoon and will tell you more than any staffing benchmark.

Whatever survives the repeat test is your actual IT strategy.

Pull your last 50 help desk tickets and mark the ones that repeated. That repetitive tier is something to buy as a service. What remains — identity, cloud spend, vendor sprawl, deciding what AI tools are allowed to reach — is what you are genuinely hiring for.

One caution: once automation absorbs the easy tier, ticket volume stops measuring how hard the job is. Judge the queue by difficulty, not count.

claims_audit: ANALYSIS: automation and self-service have removed the repetitive tier of IT work (resets, provisioning, reimaging) rather than IT roles — stated as analysis, no external statistic cited, verifiable by the reader in their own queue
ANALYSIS: as the easy tier leaves the queue, ticket volume falls while average ticket difficulty rises, making ticket count a poor staffing and pricing signal — stated as analysis, no number attached

ANALYSIS: judgment-tier work (identity architecture, Microsoft 365 permission design, cloud spend ownership, incident decisions, AI agent scope and machine identity ownership) does not compress and is harder to recruit for
OPINION: reading 50 raw tickets teaches more than a staffing benchmark
SCENARIO: the 60-person Los Angeles firm on Facebook is explicitly labelled a composite in the copy itself — no client named, implied, or described
FACT(F012): Pro Link Systems has served Los Angeles businesses since 1999, from Woodland Hills (GBP, Instagram slide 7 footer)
FACT(F002): the help desk is in-house, not outsourced (GBP)
FACT(F008): the help desk is US-based (GBP)

REMOVED: F004 (90% first-contact resolution) deliberately dropped from all channels — the post's thesis is that ticket metrics mismeasure IT work, so citing our own ticket metric would undercut the argument and overweight a single proof point
No industry statistic, incident, vulnerability, regulation, deadline, certification, partnership, or competitor appears anywhere in the package

board_findings.finding: The LinkedIn post ends with a promotional pivot ('our help desk is in-house and US-based, and 90% of tickets are resolved on first contact') that converts an otherwise peer-to-peer argument into a vendor pitch in its final beat. Worse, it is self-contradicting: the post argues ticket metrics mislead, then closes with a ticket metric. Cut the close entirely — the argument sells better without it.

The Instagram hook slide ('Four things to check before your next IT hire') is a listicle promise, not an idea. The genuinely swipe-earning line is already in the package — 'Automation didn't take IT jobs. It took the bottom tier of IT work.' Slide 1 and slide 2 currently say the same thing twice, wasting the strongest asset.

No slide in the deck is designed to be anything but a headline-plus-paragraph. A seven-slide run of identical typographic layouts reads as a template, not editorial design. At least one slide should be a structural comparison (Buy / Hire) that an art director can set as a two-column diagram rather than prose.
LinkedIn runs roughly 1,940 characters against a 900–1,600 ceiling. It is over the channel spec and the overage is the weakest material — the restated staffing paragraph and the promotional close.

The draft stops at a true but incomplete observation. The consequence a CIO actually has to defend in a budget meeting is missing: when automation absorbs the easy tier, ticket volume falls while average difficulty rises, so both internal staffing models and per-ticket MSP pricing end up measuring the part of the work that is disappearing. That is the paragraph the post was missing.

The 'judgment tier' list is 2021-era. In 2026 the fastest-growing judgment work is scoping what an AI agent is permitted to reach and who owns the machine identity it authenticates as — that belongs on the list, and its absence is why the post reads slightly behind the calendar.

'Scripted and agent-assisted workflows' is the only AI reference and it is decorative. Either the automation is specific enough to be checkable in the reader's own queue, or it should not be invoked. Tie it to observable queue behaviour and to the new governance work it creates, which is the honest two-sided account.

The Facebook scenario — 'a 60-person firm in Culver City with one internal IT person,' with 'her' week described in detail — reads as a client anecdote. Even though the audit labels it hypothetical, the reader cannot see the audit. It must be labelled a composite in the text itself.

The X thread is three posts of the same register with no standalone-quotable line. Post two should carry the counterintuitive turn (volume down, difficulty up) so it survives being screenshotted out of the thread.

The 90% first-contact-resolution figure appears in three of five channels. Repeating one verified metric across every surface makes it read as the only proof point we have. It is stronger used sparingly — and in this specific concept, not used at all, since the post's thesis is that ticket metrics are a poor measure of IT work.

'For reference on what the repetitive tier looks like when it is run deliberately' is a 14-word throat-clear before a claim. Also 'That number exists because the repeatable work was engineered to be repeatable' is circular. Both go with the cut close. GBP additionally carries two closing moves (fact block plus offer); only one may stand as the CTA.
